svg.aria-label: The Six Questions a Reader Has showing the sections that answer them and which of those can be checked by a program
svg.title: The Six Questions a Reader Has
svg.text: The Six Questions a Reader Has
In the order they have them. Green sections can be checked by a program; blue ones need a person.
1. What does this do?
Two sentences, before anything else. A reader who cannot answer
this stops reading.
2. How do I install it?
Exact commands, not a description of commands.
CHECKABLE: does each command exist?
3. How do I run it, and what should I see?
Expected output, so success is distinguishable from failure.
CHECKABLE: does it match a real capture?
4. How does it fit together?
Enough architecture to reason about a problem. What a reader
cannot recover from the code is WHY it is shaped this way.
5. What can it NOT do?
Stated, not implied. The section people skip.
CHECKABLE: against a list you maintain
6. What do I do when it breaks?
The failures you already know about — which is most of the
failures a new reader will hit.
A demo that hides its limits spends trust it has to earn back later.
Question 5 costs the least to answer and buys the most, because it is what makes the other five credible. The person who
discovers the limitation you left out will discover it at the worst possible moment, and will then re-read everything else
you wrote with suspicion.
